topic: Day 1 · Non-Variceal, Non-Ulcer Upper GI Bleeds
speakerAffiliation: Virtual Teaching Hospital · Gastroenterology & Emergency Endoscopy
speakerBio: A therapeutic endoscopist with a special interest in obscure and vascular GI bleeding. He teaches that the behaviour of a bleed names its source — and that one diagnosis must never be missed.
lectureHTML:
🎯 Where we start

A 74-year-old man with a repaired abdominal aortic aneurysm three years ago presents with a single moderate haematemesis that stops on its own. Observations normalise, the junior is reassured, and he is booked for a routine daytime endoscopy. Six hours later he exsanguinates. The scope that never happened in time would have been the wrong test anyway. This session is the 'everything else' of upper GI bleeding — the tears, the hidden arteries, the vascular malformations — and the one diagnosis whose 'herald bleed' you must never, ever dismiss.

1 · The one sentence that holds the whole topic

When it isn't an ulcer and isn't a varix, the bleed is telling you where it comes from by how it behaves — the retch, the torrent from normal mucosa, the chronic iron-deficiency ooze, or the 'small' herald bleed that precedes catastrophe.

2 · Mallory–Weiss tear — the retch-then-blood story 🤮

  • Mechanism: a longitudinal mucosal tear at the gastro-oesophageal junction caused by a sudden rise in intragastric pressure — classically retching or vomiting first, then haematemesis (the history is the diagnosis). Precipitants: alcohol binge, hyperemesis, bulimia.
  • Behaviour: usually self-limiting — ~80–90% stop spontaneously. Contrast with Boerhaave syndrome, the far rarer full-thickness rupture causing mediastinitis — a surgical emergency, not a bleed.
  • Therapy: supportive; endoscopic haemostasis (clip, adrenaline + thermal, or band) only for the minority actively bleeding at endoscopy. PPI adjunct. Rebleeding is uncommon.

3 · Dieulafoy lesion — the hidden torrential artery 🎯

  • Mechanism: an abnormally large-calibre submucosal artery that erodes through a tiny defect in otherwise normal mucosa — no ulcer around it. Usually high on the lesser curve within 6 cm of the GOJ, but can occur anywhere.
  • Behaviour: torrential, often recurrent haematemesis/melaena, frequently with a normal-looking stomach between bleeds — notoriously hard to find because the lesion is tiny and may not be bleeding at the moment of the scope.
  • Therapy: endoscopic — mechanical (clip / band) is preferred, often combined with adrenaline; thermal is an alternative. If not found or uncontrolled: repeat endoscopy, angiographic embolisation, or surgery. Tattoo the site once found (it may need re-treatment).
💡 Pearl — normal mucosa, massive bleed = think Dieulafoy

A patient with recurrent large-volume haemorrhage and a repeatedly 'normal' endoscopy is a Dieulafoy until proven otherwise. Re-scope during active bleeding to catch the spurting pinpoint vessel; mark it with a tattoo when found.

4 · Angiodysplasia & GAVE — the vascular ooze 🍉

  • Angiodysplasia: acquired arteriovenous malformations — dilated, thin-walled vessels — anywhere in the GI tract. Associated with ageing, chronic kidney disease, aortic stenosis (Heyde syndrome: AS + acquired von Willebrand deficiency + GI angiodysplasia bleeding), and von Willebrand disease. Cause chronic iron-deficiency anaemia or overt bleeding.
  • GAVE ('watermelon stomach'): gastric antral vascular ectasia — parallel red stripes of ectatic vessels radiating across the antrum like watermelon rind. Associated with cirrhosis, autoimmune/connective-tissue disease, CKD. Presents as chronic transfusion-dependent iron-deficiency anaemia. Distinct from portal hypertensive gastropathy — GAVE does not respond to portal-pressure reduction; PHG does.
  • Therapy: argon plasma coagulation (APC) is the workhorse for both angiodysplasia and GAVE (often repeated sessions). Refractory GAVE: endoscopic band ligation or radiofrequency ablation. Iron replacement; consider octreotide/thalidomide for diffuse refractory angiodysplasia.
🎯 Contrast — GAVE vs portal hypertensive gastropathy (PHG)

Both occur in cirrhotics and both ooze, but the treatment diverges completely. GAVE (antral 'watermelon' stripes) is not driven by portal pressure — treat it endoscopically (APC); TIPS/beta-blockers don't help. PHG (mosaic 'snakeskin' mucosa, usually proximal) is pressure-driven — treat it by lowering portal pressure (non-selective beta-blockers, TIPS). Getting this wrong means APC-ing a pressure problem or beta-blocking an ectasia.

5 · Cameron lesions — the hiatus-hernia bleeder 🩹

  • Mechanism: linear erosions/ulcers on the mucosal folds where a large hiatus hernia is pinched by the diaphragm — mechanical trauma plus acid and local ischaemia at the diaphragmatic hiatus.
  • Behaviour: classically chronic occult bleeding → iron-deficiency anaemia, though they can bleed acutely. Easily missed on endoscopy unless the hernia is carefully inspected on retroflexion.
  • Therapy: PPI (acid suppression + healing) and iron; large symptomatic hernias with recurrent bleeding may need surgical hernia repair. Always consider Cameron lesions in an anaemic patient with a big hiatus hernia and an otherwise 'negative' work-up.

6 · Upper GI malignancy — the friable tumour 🎗️

  • Mechanism: gastric or oesophageal cancer (or, less often, GIST/lymphoma) with a friable, ulcerated, hypervascular surface that oozes or bleeds overtly.
  • Behaviour: often chronic anaemia, weight loss, early satiety, sometimes acute bleeding; may be the presenting event of the cancer.
  • Therapy: endoscopic haemostasis is often difficult and temporary — hemospray (TC-325) is particularly useful for the diffuse ooze of a malignant surface as a bridge. Definitive control may need radiotherapy, angiographic embolisation, or surgery/oncological management. Always biopsy a suspicious lesion (once bleeding permits) and re-scope gastric ulcers to exclude malignancy.

7 · Aortoenteric fistula — the can't-miss diagnosis ☠️

The reason this session exists. An abnormal communication between the aorta and the GI tract (classically the third/fourth part of the duodenum).

  • Secondary AEF (commonest): after previous aortic graft repair (open or endovascular) — the graft erodes into the duodenum, months to years later.
  • Primary AEF: a native aortic aneurysm eroding into bowel — rarer.
  • The 'herald bleed': a self-limiting, often modest 'sentinel' GI bleed that stops spontaneously — followed hours to days later by catastrophic exsanguination. The initial bleed lulls the unwary into a false sense of security. This is the trap.
  • Diagnosis: requires a high index of suspicion in anyone with a prior aortic graft and GI bleeding. Endoscopy is often non-diagnostic (the fistula is beyond the reach/timing of a standard scope, or bleeding has stopped) and can waste critical time. CT angiography is the investigation of choice — look for perigraft gas, fluid, or contrast extravasation.
  • Management: a surgical/vascular emergency — urgent vascular surgery input; do not be reassured by a stopped bleed or a normal scope.
⚠️ Danger — 'the bleeding stopped' is not reassurance in AEF

In a patient with a prior aortic graft, a GI bleed that settles on its own is the herald bleed — the fistula has temporarily tamponaded and will re-open catastrophically. Any UGIB in a patient with an aortic graft is an aortoenteric fistula until CT angiography and vascular surgery say otherwise. Never send them for a 'routine' scope in the morning.

8 · Master table — lesion → clue → therapy 🗺️

LesionThe clue (signature)First-line therapy
Mallory–Weiss tearRetch/vomit first, then haematemesis; GOJ tear; self-limitingSupportive; clip/thermal only if actively bleeding; PPI
Dieulafoy lesionTorrential, recurrent bleed from normal mucosa; hard to findEndoscopic mechanical (clip/band) ± adrenaline; embolisation if fails; tattoo
AngiodysplasiaIron-deficiency/ overt bleed; CKD, aortic stenosis (Heyde)APC; iron; octreotide/thalidomide if diffuse refractory
GAVE'Watermelon' antral stripes; transfusion-dependent anaemia; cirrhosisAPC (repeated) / band / RFA; not portal-pressure reduction
Cameron lesionsLinear erosions in a hiatus hernia; chronic iron-deficiency anaemiaPPI + iron; hernia repair if recurrent
Upper GI malignancyWeight loss, anaemia, friable mass; chronic oozeHemospray bridge; RT / embolisation / oncology; biopsy
Aortoenteric fistulaPrior aortic graft + 'herald bleed' that stops then exsanguinatesCT angiography + emergency vascular surgery

9 · A structured approach to the 'other' UGIB 🧭

  1. Take the history that localises: retching-then-blood (Mallory–Weiss), prior aortic graft (AEF until excluded), chronic anaemia + big hiatus hernia (Cameron), transfusion-dependent ooze (GAVE/angiodysplasia), weight loss (malignancy).
  2. Recurrent big bleeds with a 'normal' scope → re-scope during bleeding for a Dieulafoy; consider CT angiography/tagged-RBC or capsule if endoscopy repeatedly negative.
  3. Match therapy to lesion (master table): mechanical for arteries, APC for ectasias, PPI/iron for erosions, surgery for AEF.
  4. Never anchor on 'the bleeding stopped' in a graft patient — image the aorta.
☠️ M&M — "It was only a small bleed"

A 74-year-old man with an open AAA repair four years earlier had a single 300 mL haematemesis in the evening that stopped spontaneously; his observations and haemoglobin were reassuring and a bedside OGD showed only a little altered blood and no clear source in the stomach or proximal duodenum. He was labelled 'settled upper GI bleed, ?gastritis' and listed for a repeat scope the next day. At 04:00 he had a massive haematemesis, arrested, and died before he reached theatre. Post-mortem: a secondary aortoenteric fistula between the graft and the third part of the duodenum — beyond the reach of the earlier scope. Errors: (1) the herald bleed was mistaken for a minor self-limiting bleed — in a graft patient it is the opposite, a warning of imminent exsanguination; (2) reliance on a standard OGD, which cannot reliably reach or exclude a distal-duodenal fistula, instead of CT angiography; (3) no vascular surgery referral. Lesson: any GI bleed in a patient with a prior aortic graft is an aortoenteric fistula until CT angiography and a vascular surgeon prove otherwise — the stopped bleed is the reason to act faster, not slower.

10 · Take-home wiring diagram

  • Mallory–Weiss: retch then blood; GOJ tear; usually self-limiting — supportive, clip only if actively bleeding.
  • Dieulafoy: big submucosal artery through normal mucosa — torrential, recurrent, hard to find; mechanical endoscopic therapy, re-scope during bleeding, tattoo.
  • Angiodysplasia / GAVE: vascular ooze → iron-deficiency anaemia; APC is the workhorse. GAVE ('watermelon') does not respond to portal-pressure reduction (unlike PHG).
  • Cameron lesions: linear erosions in a hiatus hernia → chronic iron-deficiency; PPI + iron, repair if recurrent.
  • Malignancy: friable tumour, chronic anaemia/weight loss; hemospray bridge, biopsy, oncological/RT/embolisation control.
  • Aortoenteric fistula: prior aortic graft + herald bleed = can't-miss. CT angiography, emergency vascular surgery; never be reassured by a stopped bleed or a normal scope.

Simple enough to remember: the bleed's behaviour names its source. Impossible to forget: in a graft patient, 'the bleeding stopped' is the herald, not the all-clear.

moderatorQs.q: A patient has had three large haematemeses but two endoscopies were reported as normal. What is your leading diagnosis and how do you pursue it?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: The leading diagnosis is a Dieulafoy lesion — an abnormally large-calibre submucosal artery that erodes through a pinpoint defect in otherwise normal mucosa, producing torrential, recurrent bleeding yet a near-normal-looking stomach between bleeds, which is exactly why it is missed. The strategy is to re-scope during active bleeding to catch the spurting pinpoint vessel (often high on the lesser curve within 6 cm of the GOJ), inspecting meticulously with washing and retroflexion. When found, treat with mechanical haemostasis (clip or band, often with adrenaline) and tattoo the site because recurrence is common. If repeated endoscopy remains negative, escalate to CT angiography or catheter angiography (which may show the vessel and allow embolisation), tagged-RBC scan, or capsule/enteroscopy to exclude a more distal source.

moderatorQs.q: How do you distinguish GAVE from portal hypertensive gastropathy, and why does it matter therapeutically?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: It matters because the treatments are opposite. GAVE (gastric antral vascular ectasia, 'watermelon stomach') appears as red ectatic stripes radiating across the antrum and causes chronic transfusion-dependent iron-deficiency anaemia; crucially it is not driven by portal pressure, so it does not respond to beta-blockers or TIPS — it is treated endoscopically with argon plasma coagulation (repeated), or band ligation/RFA if refractory. Portal hypertensive gastropathy (PHG) shows a mosaic 'snakeskin' pattern, usually in the proximal stomach/fundus, and is pressure-driven, so it responds to portal-pressure reduction (non-selective beta-blockers, TIPS). Confusing them leads to APC-ing a pressure problem or beta-blocking an ectasia — both fail. The antral 'watermelon' distribution versus proximal 'mosaic', and response (or not) to portal decompression, separate them.

moderatorQs.q: Why is a normal upper GI endoscopy potentially dangerous reassurance in a patient with a previous aortic graft?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Because an aortoenteric fistula classically communicates with the third or fourth part of the duodenum, which is at or beyond the reach of a standard OGD, and the fistula frequently is not actively bleeding at the time of the scope (it tamponades transiently — the 'herald bleed'). A normal or non-diagnostic endoscopy therefore does not exclude AEF and, worse, wastes critical time and falsely reassures. In any patient with a prior aortic graft (open or endovascular) presenting with GI bleeding — especially a self-limiting sentinel bleed — the working diagnosis must be AEF until CT angiography (looking for perigraft gas, fluid or contrast extravasation) and a vascular surgeon say otherwise. This is a surgical emergency; the stopped bleed is a warning of imminent exsanguination, not an all-clear.

audienceQs.q: A young woman came in with haematemesis after a night of vomiting from a stomach bug. She's stable now — how worried should I be?
audienceQs.answerHTML: This is the classic story of a Mallory–Weiss tear: a bout of retching/vomiting first, then haematemesis, from a longitudinal mucosal tear at the gastro-oesophageal junction. The reassuring news is that ~80–90% are self-limiting and settle with supportive care and a PPI; endoscopic haemostasis (clip, or adrenaline plus thermal, or band) is only needed for the minority found actively bleeding, and rebleeding is uncommon. So a haemodynamically stable patient can often be managed conservatively. The two things to keep in mind: (1) confirm she is genuinely stable with serial observations and haemoglobin, and (2) remember the rare, dangerous mimic — Boerhaave syndrome, a full-thickness oesophageal rupture presenting with severe chest/abdominal pain and sepsis rather than simple bleeding — which is a surgical emergency, not a Mallory–Weiss tear.

audienceQs.q: We keep transfusing an elderly man with aortic stenosis for recurrent iron-deficiency anaemia and no obvious source — any GI angle?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Yes — think Heyde syndrome: the triad of aortic stenosis, acquired von Willebrand deficiency, and bleeding GI angiodysplasia. The high shear stress across the stenotic valve cleaves large von Willebrand multimers, producing an acquired coagulopathy that unmasks bleeding from angiodysplastic lesions (acquired arteriovenous malformations common in the elderly and in CKD). Practically: pursue the angiodysplasia endoscopically — argon plasma coagulation is the mainstay, with iron replacement, and octreotide or thalidomide considered for diffuse refractory disease. Critically, the definitive treatment of Heyde syndrome is often aortic valve replacement, which corrects the von Willebrand defect and frequently resolves the recurrent GI bleeding. So loop in cardiology to assess the valve rather than simply transfusing indefinitely.

audienceQs.q: An anaemic patient with a big hiatus hernia has had two negative bleeding work-ups. What are we missing?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Very likely Cameron lesions — linear erosions or ulcers on the gastric folds where a large hiatus hernia is mechanically pinched by the diaphragmatic hiatus, injured by a combination of mechanical trauma, acid and local ischaemia. They characteristically cause chronic occult blood loss and iron-deficiency anaemia rather than dramatic bleeding, and they are easily overlooked unless the endoscopist specifically inspects the hernia sac, including on retroflexion — which is why the work-up can be falsely 'negative.' Management is PPI therapy (acid suppression to heal the erosions) plus iron replacement; for large symptomatic hernias with recurrent or transfusion-dependent bleeding, surgical hiatus hernia repair is definitive. So the next step is a targeted repeat endoscopy looking explicitly at the hernia neck, and correcting the iron deficiency meanwhile.
